title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1), executed, and archived a sealed synthetic benchmark and a deterministic snapshot validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on intent→configuration tasks. The confirmatory paired design used N=300 tasks (4 intent clusters, 75 tasks/cluster) with a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions received the same initial candidate; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one automated repair per task only when the deterministic validator failed. Declared model: gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). Provider accounting: 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly 1 repair call (model_calls_used = 301; stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 1). Primary outcomes: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (target effect = 0.10) was not supported. The null result is explained by a ceiling baseline and minimal GVR engagement (one repair invocation). The single discordant episode and the single repair provider trace are recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); auditors should extract the per‑episode entry there for the episode identifier and repair trace. We release the preregistration, full execution manifest, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support community extensions.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, change planning, remediation). Prior work reports promise but also frequent syntax, topology, and semantic errors when LLM outputs are applied directly to network devices. Deterministic verification and iterative repair---a generate–validate–repair (GVR) architecture---is often proposed to reduce operational risk, but the community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that (a) pair operational intents with deterministic correctness specifications and (b) permit sealed confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines versus single‑pass generation. We address that gap with a sealed experiment that (1) delivers a reusable synthetic task bank and validator, (2) preregisters a paired confirmatory design (ac-2026-003-prereg-v1), and (3) reports a machine‑auditable execution and analysis comparing a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator under a constrained repair budget. The final research question was: under fixed seeds and at most one repair call per task, does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM? Our contributions are (i) a machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator with sealed preregistration; (ii) a paired experimental execution with complete provider accounting and per‑task validator traces; and (iii) artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark designs that can reveal repair value.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and focused studies document rapid growth in investigations of LLMs for network operations, but they also highlight shortcomings in reproducible, operationally meaningful evaluation. Comprehensive reviews summarize opportunities and open challenges in applying LLMs to NetOps (e.g., Long et al., 2025; Hong et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024) and case studies demonstrate that verifier‑assisted generation and localized repair can reduce misconfigurations in limited settings (e.g., Mondal et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024). Complementary work documents prompt injection, jailbreak, and hallucination risks relevant to operational automation. Collectively these prior findings motivated our sealed, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison that fixes generator variance via a shared‑initial design and isolates the incremental value of automated repair under a tightly constrained budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary hypothesis. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution. Primary hypothesis H1 (confirmatory): the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration specifies task composition, validator semantics, model and adapter configuration, exclusion/missingness rules, stopping rules, and the exact analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The preregistration and its SHA‑256 are archived in the evidence bundle.

Task bank and validator semantics. A deterministic task generator produced 300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, and an explicit required_sequence. Tasks vary in device counts (3–50) and abstract multi‑vendor device models. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements full_intent_constraint_validation: snapshot semantics that accept a candidate only if all declared constraints and required sequences are satisfied and enumerate violation codes otherwise. The validator is deterministic and stateless by design to produce unambiguous binary pass/fail outcomes for confirmatory testing.

Paired design and shared‑initial semantics. To tightly control generator variance we used a shared‑initial generation per task: a single generation call produced the shared candidate that served as the baseline single‑pass output; for the guarded condition the same shared candidate is validated and only if it failed could the GVR pipeline issue up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Planned_episode_count was 600 (300 shared initial + up to 300 repairs). This design isolates repair efficacy: any guarded improvement must derive from an invoked repair rather than a different initial sample. Provider accounting and per‑call traces were archived to verify stage_counts and per‑episode behavior.

Model and runtime configuration. Declared/requested model: "gpt-5-mini"; provider: "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null; the hosted adapter operated in deterministic sampling mode. For reproducibility, the authoritative model_configuration.json is archived (execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and the full raw_results index (including the single repair provider trace and the discordant episode entry) is archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl, SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d). The immutable initial master prompt reference is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproduction requires using these archived artifacts and the per‑call provider traces; bit‑for‑bit reproduction also requires access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archive.

Analysis plan. The preregistered estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The pre-specified test is exact McNemar two‑sided; we also compute a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Pre-specified sensitivity treatments for missingness/exclusions were registered; no exclusions or missing pairs occurred.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600; completed_episode_count = 600; complete_pair_count = 300; failed_episode_count = 0; model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}. All per‑call provider traces and validator diagnostics are archived for audit.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated successes: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Table 1 summarizes these counts and statistics.

Statistical note on p = 1.0. The McNemar exact two‑sided p‑value derives from the discordant pair counts: with only one discordant pair (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) the two‑sided enumeration yields p = 1.0; practically this reflects that the observed single discordance is consistent with chance under the null given the discrete paired sample. Coupled with the near‑ceiling baseline, the design had no realistic opportunity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10). See the preregistration sensitivity routine and post‑hoc arithmetic in the archive for precise power recalibration.

Representative artifacts and diagnostics. The archived bundle includes per‑task scoring JSONs and shared initial responses (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json … task-000006-guarded.json) that illustrate validator traces (normalized_configuration, required_command_count, final_state). Many tasks required multi‑step sequences (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). The single repair invocation and the discordant episode entry are present in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d); auditors should extract the episode identifier and the repair provider trace from that file. The model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820) and task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256: 062b80216e49a2919ebf8debd75cf02fffcfd752b5b253e5a11c0701ca853097) are authoritative for reproducing the run.

Tables. Table 1: confirmatory counts and statistics (n11, n10, n01, n00; rates; paired difference; bootstrap CI; McNemar p). Table 2: preregistered task‑bank composition (intent clusters and counts) and shared‑initial design summary.
sections.discussion:
Null outcome diagnosis. The confirmatory null result should be interpreted narrowly: on this synthetic task bank, with deterministic sampling producing highly correct shared candidates (299/300), and with repair restricted to validator failures and at most one repair call per task, the guarded pipeline had almost no opportunity to differ from baseline. Two linked causes explain the null: (1) a near‑ceiling baseline leaves no room to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10), and (2) the repair trigger policy engaged only once (stage_counts: repair = 1), so repair efficacy could not be exercised. These instrumentally grounded facts are directly observable in the archived execution accounting and per‑task validator traces.

Concrete benchmark recommendations. Artifact‑grounded lessons lead to concrete design choices when the research goal is to evaluate repair value: (A) increase task difficulty or include adversarial seeding to raise initial failure rates; (B) allow iterative repairs (multiple repair attempts per failed candidate) so localized fixes can accumulate; (C) include multiple independent generations per task as baseline samples to quantify generator variance and selection benefits; (D) deploy stateful or temporal validators (execution emulation) rather than purely snapshot checks to surface ordering and side‑effect errors. Each recommendation directly follows from execution accounting (300 shared initial generations; a single repair invocation) and the per‑task validator diagnostics archived in the execution bundle.

Reproducibility and deterministic sampling. The hosted adapter used deterministic sampling settings (temperature unset; adapter deterministic mode) to ensure repeatable shared‑initial outputs under the recorded provider conditions. Practically, reproducing identical outputs requires: (i) the archived model_configuration.json (SHA‑256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820); (ii) the raw_results.jsonl index (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) that contains per‑call provider traces and the single repair provider trace; and (iii) access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics as recorded. We intentionally archived the initial_master_prompt_reference (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) so auditors can verify the exact prompt used by the autonomous pipeline.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design deliberately controls generator variance but also creates a dependency: repair can only act upon a single sampled candidate. Construct validity: the deterministic snapshot validator enforces explicit intent constraints but omits temporal execution dynamics and vendor CLI idiosyncrasies. External validity: tasks are synthetic and device models abstracted; only gpt-5-mini and one validator were evaluated. Conclusion validity: the near‑ceiling baseline and the single discordant pair limit inferential power for the preregistered target effect; planned exploratory failure clustering is underpowered with n10=1. All of these threats are traceable to archived artifacts and are discussed and quantified in the release.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Observed pass rates were near perfect (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR would produce a materially higher pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported. Execution accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once (stage_counts: repair = 1), so automated repair rarely differed from baseline; this limited engagement explains the null confirmatory outcome. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable community extensions (harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, multi‑generation baselines, multi‑model comparisons) that can more powerfully evaluate when and how GVR pipelines provide operational value.

limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about GVR practical superiority.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 300, repair = 1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10 = 1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model_configuration.json and the per‑call provider traces archived in the execution bundle.

Artifact note: the single repair provider trace and the identifier of the single discordant episode are present in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256: 0d841d29dd190ebe50a1973b0eabfd8801bf81476d395b417145fb5201a5511d) and are authoritative for auditors.
